summary.summary: Barnet's borrowing is scaling fast: having historically funded capital spending from internal cash, the council borrowed a further £159.44m in 2025/26, lifting total debt from £1.157bn to £1.317bn, with another £49.36m of existing debt refinanced in-year. Treasury investments fell to £49.875m (from £61.621m) — described as 'broadly at the council's liquidity buffer', the minimum cash its strategy allows — and the report acknowledges managing 'relatively low cash balances' through a volatile rate environment. Outside the treasury book sit £422.731m of non-treasury investments, including loans to council-owned subsidiaries, third-party developers and community organisations, plus gilts held against Brent Cross Plot 1 commercial agreements. Loan-level detail, the CFR and the maturity ladder are in Appendix A, presented with the outturn to Cabinet on 9 June 2026.

signals.headline: £159.44m borrowed in 2025/26, taking total debt from £1.157bn to £1.317bn (+14%), the second year of heavy external borrowing since the internal-funding era ended in 2024/25
signals.why: Barnet has become a large, recurring borrower whose capital programme now depends on continuous access to PWLB and market debt.

signals.headline: Treasury investments of £49.875m at 31 March 2026 were 'broadly at the council's liquidity buffer' — the lowest cash holding its strategy permits — down from £61.621m a year earlier
signals.why: Sitting at the floor means any cash-flow shock converts directly into new short-term borrowing.

signals.headline: £422.731m of non-treasury investments outstanding at 31 March 2026, including loans to local-authority-owned subsidiaries, third-party developers and community organisations
signals.why: A sum equal to a third of the council's debt is lent outside the treasury strategy's safeguards, with repayment resting on developers' and subsidiaries' performance.

news_drafts.headline: Barnet cuts its Exceptional Financial Support requirement by £6m to £73.298m
news_drafts.lead:
Barnet Council's requirement for exceptional financial support, government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending, has fallen by £6m to £73.298m, from the £79.298m approved. The figure is in the chief finance officer's quarter 2 forecast for 2026/27, put to the Finance and Growth Overview and Scrutiny Sub-Committee on 12 November 2026.

The paper gives two reasons for the reduction: a better-than-expected 2025/26 outturn of £5m, and £1m of additional parking income in 2026/27. It says the support is met from borrowing. Separately, £5m of contingency carried forward from 2025/26 "is not expected to be needed and will be used to reduce the EFS requirement". Of the £34.967m contingency budget for 2026/27, £28.078m is earmarked for services or to reduce the support, leaving £6.889m for the rest of the year. The contingency includes £4.304m carried forward from 2025/26.

At the sub-committee's meeting on 8 October 2026, a member noted that the support is predicted to fall close to zero in 2031-32 and asked whether it would be repaid by then. The council's Executive Director of Finance said the council "is allowed to repay the EFS over 20 years, so this meant that no new EFS is being budgeted for by 2031-32". Repayments and interest are built into the budget and held in the Capital Adjustment Account.
news_drafts.paper_title: Annex A Chief Finance Officer Report 202627 Q2 Financial Forecast and 202627 Budget Management

news_drafts.headline: Barnet pension fund's 2025/26 draft accounts need three adjustments, including £2.626m of expenses
news_drafts.lead:
The external auditor has identified three adjustments to the draft 2025/26 financial statements of Barnet's pension fund, according to its audit findings report, which went to the Local Pension Board on 19 October 2026. Management expenses were overstated by £2.626m, a figure found through management's own review. A separate adjustment concerns the value of investments.

For investments, the auditor found a £1.495m difference between the value in the statements and the value later confirmed by the fund managers. The report says this arose from timing: the managers' confirmations were not available when the draft was prepared, so management "used the best available information at that time". The third adjustment is a £76k overpayment.

The report also covers a bank reconciliation problem carried over from the previous year. Of an £841k cash balance from West Yorkshire Pension Fund, £562k could not be reconciled. Management told the auditor the reconciliation is "still ongoing". The auditor said the difference is not material and it proposed no audit adjustment. It still described this as "a significant weakness in the reconciliation process". Prior-year corrections also included £2.1m of cash in transit that was not initially recorded, and an £8k US dollar account balance that had been left out of the general ledger.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 2 Audit Findings Report 2025-26 - Sent to Management

news_drafts.headline: Barnet Cabinet papers: £200m benefits target by 2029/30, with government borrowing support still planned
news_drafts.lead:
Barnet Council delivered 95.8% of its planned savings in 2025/26, stayed within its agreed budget and used about £10m less Exceptional Financial Support than government had approved, according to papers for its Cabinet meeting on 12 October. That support is government permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, a last resort. The council had £55.7m approved for 2025/26 and used £45.9m. The papers say tighter control of spending, recruitment and agency costs since 2024 has improved its forecasting.

The council has set a target of £200m in financial benefits by 2029/30, against a forecast budget gap of £198m. Its Financial Sustainability Plan aims to end reliance on the support by March 2029 through five themes, including prevention, productivity and income growth. The current medium-term financial strategy, the council's multi-year financial plan, includes no savings from that plan yet. Projects will be added once they have business cases, a named owner and delivery milestones.

For 2026/27, government has approved in principle support of up to £79.6m, of which £73.6m is expected to be needed. The council is seeking approval for 2027/28, and the papers say support is likely to remain necessary then and possibly in 2028/29. Financing costs of the borrowing, interest plus the minimum revenue provision (the amount set aside each year to repay past borrowing), rise from £9.6m in 2027/28 to £22.6m in 2030/31, totalling £62.75m over the period.

findings.headline: Adult social care debt rose £1.067m to £26.164m, with £22.007m over 90 days old.
findings.detail: NHS North Central London ICB is the largest debtor at £7.685m, of which £7.243m is over 90 days. Since Q1 the council received £3.3m from the ICB, and £5.2m relates to two invoices from February 2026 still under discussion.
findings.matters: Health-body debt over 90 days is a counterparty exposure that a lender or a finance director at a council with similar integrated-care income would want to see.

daily_post.headline: Non-treasury investments increased 30% to £372.856m with governance acknowledged as absent and under review
daily_post.lead: Large non-treasury investments outside normal Treasury Management governance creates potential reporting, oversight and reputational risk. The explicit acknowledgement that governance is absent indicates the council recognises a gap in its control framework.
